Acoma Pueblo

Acoma is a living Pueblo community whose own histories place Haak’u at the center of a continuing homeland. Its public sources connect the mesa settlement, Spanish colonial encounters, language work, and the stewardship of buildings and cultural records. Community institutions provide a fuller picture than the familiar image of an ancient village alone.

Names & relationshipsAcoma is an individual Pueblo community. Pueblo is also a broader regional term; it does not identify a single government or language shared by all Pueblo peoples.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

Haak’u and historical time

Acoma’s own introduction describes Haak’u as a homeland understood through oral history and emergence. It separately discusses archaeological evidence and continuous occupation from at least about AD 1200. These are different forms of historical knowledge, with different questions and methods. The date of an excavated deposit does not define the beginning of Acoma identity. The Pueblo’s account should therefore be read on its own terms alongside archaeological research, rather than reduced to a contest over the oldest settlement.

Read the sources [1] Pueblo of Acoma

02

Colonial history and rebuilding

The Pueblo’s rebuilding account describes conflicts over Spanish colonial authority, complaints about abuses, and the expansion of Franciscan mission activity. It places Fray Juan Ramirez’s arrival in 1629 within that history. San Esteban del Rey subsequently became an enduring structure at Acoma, but the Pueblo’s modern account explicitly treats the mission as one chapter in a much larger community history. Its survival reflects the labor and choices of Acoma people across generations.

Read the sources [2] Pueblo of Acoma [3] Pueblo of Acoma

03

Preservation as community work

The Tribal Council and administration created Acoma’s historic-preservation office in 1999. Its public description includes archives, archaeological protection, consultation, and work concerning repatriation. Restoration has involved traditional leadership and the church caretakers, known as gaugashti, alongside training in building methods. Preservation here is an active community responsibility, bringing documentary records, structures, and learning together. The office’s description is also a direct route to understanding the Pueblo’s own priorities for protecting its heritage.

Read the sources [4] Pueblo of Acoma [3] Pueblo of Acoma

04

Language and controlled access

The H’aakume Dzeeni Language Program describes work on a Keres dictionary begun in 2017, with fluent speakers editing conversational vocabulary and phrases used in Acoma, McCartys, and Acomita. Its goals connect resources for learners with school and home use. The program explicitly excludes culturally sensitive words and seeks access controls for tribal members. Public information about this work is an invitation to understand language continuity, not permission to seek or reproduce restricted teaching materials.

Read the sources [5] Pueblo of Acoma

05

Education and continuing life

Acoma’s modern history places language retention, historic preservation, and higher education together. The language program likewise presents learning as a responsibility toward children and future generations. These accounts show how cultural continuity depends on institutions, family participation, and sustained work. They also remind readers to distinguish an institutional project description from a completed outcome: a dictionary project or preservation plan is evidence of an effort, not proof that every goal has already been achieved.

What needs further research

  • Add specialist sources on the 1599 assault, colonial labor, and the Pueblo Revolt with precise historical citations.
  • Expand land, water, governance, and contemporary arts coverage through Acoma-authored accounts.
